confidence_note: The old TR text described a vague photo-and-statistics experiment with no names; that version could not be tied to the book. Replaced with the Sheri Summers experiment (Batson and colleagues, 1995), which Bloom discusses in Against Empathy; details come from secondary sources (Freakonomics transcript, reviews), not the book text. Group design is described only as high-empathy versus low-empathy. 'Statistics fade' / 'dullness of statistics' wording is not used. Individual researcher first names and exact sample sizes omitted.
facts: Batson and colleagues ran an experiment in 1995, which Paul Bloom discusses in Against Empathy.
Volunteers learned about Sheri Summers, a ten-year-old with a fatal disease who was waiting for treatment.
They were asked whether to move her up the waiting list so she would get immediate treatment.
Moving her up meant other children waiting for treatment would be pushed back.
One group was first asked to imagine what Sheri felt, to put themselves in her shoes (high empathy). A comparison group was not (low empathy).
About three-quarters of the high-empathy group wanted to move her up. About one-third of the low-empathy group did.
Bloom uses the result to argue that empathy focuses on one person and can push people to treat others unfairly.
scene_details: a ten-year-old named Sheri Summers on a waiting list for treatment
the instruction: imagine what she feels
tension: The same girl and the same list produce opposite answers depending on whether volunteers were told to imagine her feelings.
opening_idea: Start with Sheri Summers, a ten-year-old with a fatal disease on a waiting list, and the single question put to volunteers.

lessons.idea: Feeling strongly for one person can quietly change a fair decision, because the others affected are never pictured.
lessons.anchor: Volunteers told to imagine Sheri's feelings mostly moved her up the list, which pushed other children back.

reflect_final: In a recent decision that affected several people, whose situation did you picture most vividly, and who stayed out of view?

use_cases.situation: A manager is asked to bump one colleague's request to the front of the queue after hearing a moving story.
use_cases.move: Ask who else is waiting and what each of them needs before moving anyone.

use_cases.situation: A friend pleads for you to donate to one person's fundraiser.
use_cases.move: Say you are moved, and that you first want to see where the same money helps most people.

use_cases.situation: You feel a strong pull to make an exception for one child over another.
use_cases.move: In Bloom's study, imagining Sheri's feelings moved her ahead of other children; pause and name the others affected before deciding.

pocket_idea: Imagine one person's feelings and a waiting list quietly reorders; before deciding, count the people you did not picture.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Tell people to imagine a sick girl's feelings, and three-quarters will move her ahead of other children in line.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In a 1995 experiment Paul Bloom describes, volunteers were asked whether Sheri Summers, a ten-year-old with a fatal disease, should skip ahead on a waiting list. Told to imagine her feelings, about three-quarters said yes. Without that instruction, about a third did. Bloom's point: empathy lights up one person and can leave the rest of the line unfairly behind.
